We begin with small models we can inspect, then connect molecular representations to prediction, simulation, and experimental decisions. The topic sequence below is a guide to the material; it is not one topic per meeting.

## What would you like to investigate? {#learning-goals}

Keep a running collection of project ideas alongside the practicals. Add a chemical question, possible data, a first comparison, and anything you need help with to the **shared document linked in the course email**. A rough idea is enough. We will use these notes to shape manageable projects and help people with related interests find one another.

## Time to work together {#working-together}

For the meetings after the introduction, my proposal is to begin with a short explanation or demonstration, perhaps **ten to fifteen minutes**, and spend most of our time working through examples and calculations. You can work on your own or with a partner. I will be there to help when code fails, talk through a modelling choice, or examine a result with you. Where a question affects several people, we can bring it back to the board for a few minutes.

We would finish by comparing what we found and identifying what needs another look. In a longer meeting, we can repeat this pattern around a break. The notes provide the fuller explanations to return to afterwards. Short preparation tasks can give us a starting point, but unfinished attempts are welcome and the suggested reading remains optional.

We will adjust the pace to what helps the class. The topic sequence below does not imply a full lecture on each topic before you get to try anything.

## Project and assessment {#assessment}

The Friedolin listing for **MC3.4.c, Advanced Methods in Digital Chemistry** (course 248388, winter semester 2026/27) names two assessment components:

| Component | Name in Friedolin | Examination number |
|---|---|---|
| **Project with a written report** | Projektarbeit mit schriftlicher Ausarbeitung | 319971 |
| **Final presentation with discussion** | Abschlussvortrag mit Diskussion | 319972 |

I would like you to spend most of your project time working on a question you find interesting. We will choose a scope that lets you try something, inspect the result, and explain what you learned. A careful comparison or an informative failure can give us plenty to discuss.

The written work should grow out of that investigation: the question, the calculations and figures, the choices you made, and what the evidence supports. We will discuss whether a commented notebook with a short accompanying explanation would be a useful format. The presentation can draw on the same work. The aim is to make your reasoning understandable without creating unnecessary extra work in packaging it.

We will agree a manageable scope, the form and length of the written work, the presentation, and suitable dates. These details are still open. The assessment brief, including grading criteria and any weighting, will follow once the applicable module requirements have been checked.

### Where do project ideas come from? {#project-ideas}

You do not need to arrive with a project idea. I will suggest starting points drawn from the course examples, and you can also bring a question from another course or your own research interests. We will turn the idea into a question that can be investigated with the time, data, and tools available. 

### When should we start? {#project-timing}

Collect ideas in the shared document during the practical sessions and use the calculations to find out what interests you. After those first practicals, discuss a possible question with me. A short conversation or a few sentences are enough: what would you like to find out, what data could you use, and what would you compare or check first? This is a way to get feedback on the scope, not an additional assessed report.

Start the main investigation once we have agreed a manageable question and a feasible first step. Use the supported practical time to try things and get help. You do not need to wait until we have covered every method, and you do not need to finish the project during a block week. Keep a record of your calculations, choices, and results as you go, so the report and presentation can grow out of that work.

### When is the project due? {#project-dates}

**The written-report deadline and the date of the final presentation have not yet been set.** We will discuss both alongside the course timetable, allowing time to work on the project after the relevant teaching sessions. The end of the listed lecture period is not, by itself, a project deadline.

Once the timetable and applicable requirements have been checked, I will publish the dates and submission instructions here and in the assessment brief. Please share any constraints that would affect a workable schedule. The idea collection is a starting point for discussion, not an assessed proposal.

## Learning from observations {#learning-from-observations}

We begin with a calibration curve because we can follow the whole calculation. There are only a few observations, and we know something about the experiment. When we move to a table of porous materials, the same questions remain, but even deciding what counts as a new material becomes less straightforward.

For the ML basics, we build on my [MolSim teaching material](https://www.compchem.nl/wp-content/uploads/molsim2023/L09_Machine-Learning.pdf): how to describe a system, choose and fit a function, estimate its error, and decide whether a more elaborate model helps. We work through these steps with a calibration curve, the MolSim adsorption data, and an exercise fitting an interaction energy. This gives us calculations to return to when we introduce neural networks and molecular simulation.

::: {.course-outline}

| Topic group | Topics | What we will work through |
|---|---|---|
| **1. AI, science, and our tools** | Modelling as deliberate omission; AI as an ambition; its history and methods; prediction, explanation, and causality; probability; the human choices behind models. | Classify examples and consider what a model leaves out. Use selected historical examples to place LLMs in a broader field, then examine how a changed question needs different evidence and what seven successes in ten attempts tell us. Set up an AI-assistant and a Python notebook. [Lecture notes](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd) · [Setup](setup.qmd) |
| **2. Fitting a model** | Inputs and targets; parameters and hyperparameters; losses; fitting; underfitting and overfitting; training, validation, and test data. | Calculate predictions and errors, change a calibration curve, and compare results on new observations. Establish why **test error is still an empirical estimate**. Follow up by examining bias, variance, and regularisation in the model-selection practical below. [Lecture notes](lectures/02-learning-from-data.qmd) |
| **3. Making a chemical comparison** | Predicting a value, a label, or an ordering; descriptors, baselines, and scaling; linear and kernel models; provenance, leakage, and uncertainty in an error estimate. | Predict computed CO₂ uptake, compare models using validation data, inspect residuals, and state which future cases the evaluation can describe. Use this example to ask which observations belong together in cross-validation. [Lecture notes](lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd) |

:::

The first supported practical brings these topics together in [**How should we choose a model?**](lectures/model-selection.qmd). We reuse the MolSim example of fitting a Lennard–Jones potential: repeated noisy energy values let us distinguish **bias from variance**, then investigate **regularisation** by changing a penalty while keeping the degree fixed. Finally, we use **cross-validation** to compare settings when one validation split may give a fragile comparison. We will fit preprocessing inside each fold and distinguish selecting a model from evaluating the selected procedure. For chemical data, we also ask whether folds should separate molecules, families, batches, or times. This is core material before neural networks; the formal bias–variance derivation and nested cross-validation are further depth.

By this point, we should be able to take a supplied data table, identify its target and conditions, fit a simple comparison model, justify a model-selection procedure, and explain what its reported error does and does not tell us. We need that foundation before adding more elaborate models.

During these early practicals, everyone will also have an opportunity to [try a coding assistant in the terminal](cli-assistant.qmd), on their own or with a partner. We will ask it to inspect and repair a small calculation, examine the changed file, and run checks ourselves. This uses supported time in the first modelling practicals once the Python setup and the error calculation are familiar. If setup needs longer, we will arrange a further supported opportunity without dropping the model-selection discussion.

## Representing molecules and their behaviour {#molecular-models}

So far, we have supplied descriptions of the materials and chosen the functions to fit. Next we let parts of those functions be learned, then give the models access to connectivity and geometry. This brings us to a different use of a learned model: calculating energies and forces inside a simulation.

::: {.course-outline}

| Topic group | Topics | What we will work through |
|---|---|---|
| **4. A small neural network** | Weighted sums, nonlinear functions, layers, fitting, and learned intermediate representations; training and validation curves, weight decay, and early stopping. | Calculate a small network's output by hand, modify a supplied model, and compare it with a simpler baseline under the same evaluation. Revisit overfitting and regularisation; choosing when to stop training is also a model choice. |
| **5. Molecular representations** | Molecular graphs, local environments, information passed between neighbouring atoms, and properties that should survive atom relabelling or rotation. | Follow one update on a molecular graph and inspect a supplied prediction or attribution. Distinguish explaining the model's calculation from establishing a chemical mechanism. |
| **6. Energies, forces, and simulation** | Learned potentials; forces as energy derivatives; the configurations a model has seen; numerical integration and sampling. | Draw force arrows on a potential, check a finite difference, and inspect a short supplied trajectory. Separate error in the learned potential from integration error and inadequate sampling. |

:::

By this stage, you should be able to follow how a molecular description becomes a prediction and explain which changes ought to leave that prediction unchanged. We will train a small network ourselves and use prepared models where training would consume the time we need to examine the calculation.

## From predictions to decisions {#predictions-and-decisions}

A model that predicts a property does not yet tell us which molecule to make or which experiment to perform. Those decisions introduce objectives, constraints, uncertainty, and costs. Language models give us another way to propose steps in a workflow, with further questions about how those steps are checked.

::: {.course-outline}

| Topic group | Topics | What we will work through |
|---|---|---|
| **7. Proposing molecules** | Searching an existing collection versus generating new candidates; one way to learn a distribution of molecular representations; objectives and chemical constraints. | Examine supplied candidates and compare them with a simple search. Check what validity, novelty, and a favourable predicted score actually establish, and what remains to be tested. |
| **8. Choosing the next measurement** | Predictions and their uncertainty; updating a probability model with observations; balancing promising and uncertain choices under a budget. This leads to Bayesian optimisation. | Choose the next point before its result is revealed, then compare search procedures over repeated simulated runs. Distinguish finding a good condition from estimating the causal effect of changing it. |
| **9. Language models in a research workflow** | Predicting pieces of text; training and prompting; retrieving sources; calling tools; evaluating a complete assisted task. | Check a bounded literature or chemistry task against supplied sources and executable calculations. Compare a generated explanation, a tool result, and a formally checked derivation: they establish different things. |

:::


## A result another chemist can examine {#bringing-the-work-together}

**Topic 10: reproducibility and project discussion.** We bring together the question, data, model, evaluation, and interpretation in a small piece of work. Another person should be able to run the calculation and understand the conclusion. We will exchange work, inspect one another's evidence, and explain a modelling choice and a limitation.
